findings.description: Unbounded memory allocation in IntegerPayloadDecoder via readFromStream with untrusted length parameter
findings.reasoning: The IntegerPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder method at line 145 calls readFromStream with the `length` parameter directly from the ASN.1 encoded data without validation. The length field in ASN.1 BER encoding can be arbitrarily large (up to 2^32 or more depending on encoding), and passing this directly to readFromStream can cause the substrate.read(size) call to attempt allocating excessive memory, leading to a Denial of Service attack.

evidence.code_context: The valueDecoder method receives a 'length' parameter from the ASN.1 decoder which represents the length field from the BER-encoded data. This length is passed directly to readFromStream without any bounds checking or validation.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Untrusted length from ASN.1 BER encoding → valueDecoder(length parameter) → readFromStream(substrate, length, options) → substrate.read(size) with unbounded size
evidence.notes: ASN.1 BER encoding allows length fields up to 2^32 or larger. An attacker can craft a malicious ASN.1 message with an extremely large length value to trigger memory exhaustion. The readFromStream function will attempt to read that many bytes, causing excessive memory allocation.

findings.description: Integer overflow in length calculation at line 1306 - untagged ANY decoder adds untrusted position difference to length without bounds checking
findings.code_snippet: length += currentPosition - fullPosition
findings.reasoning: At line 1306, the code performs `length += currentPosition - fullPosition` where both `currentPosition` and `fullPosition` come from substrate position tracking. These values are derived from untrusted input (the BER-encoded data stream). The subtraction `currentPosition - fullPosition` can produce a large positive value that, when added to the existing `length` variable, causes an integer overflow. This is particularly dangerous because the overflowed length value is then used in subsequent operations like `peekIntoStream(substrate, length)` at line 1309, which can lead to out-of-bounds memory access or excessive memory allocation. Python's arbitrary precision integers prevent traditional overflow wrapping, but the semantic overflow (using an unexpectedly large value for length calculations) can cause denial of service through excessive memory consumption or buffer over-reads.

evidence.notes: The vulnerability exists because there is no upper bound check on the length value after the addition. An attacker can craft a malicious BER stream where the position difference is extremely large, causing the length to become unexpectedly large and leading to resource exhaustion or out-of-bounds access.
